answer:
HYPOTHESIS (data-grounded answer to: "Is the relation between SES and chances of degree completion affected by racial lines?")

In the NLS dataset (data/nls_ses_processed.csv, N=8,773), higher SES is associated with a greater probability of BA DEGREE COMPLETED for all three values of SAMPLE_RACE (White, Black, Hispanic), but once academic background is controlled there is NO statistically reliable evidence that SAMPLE_RACE moderates the strength of the SES→degree-completion relationship.

Concretely: in the unadjusted model the SES effect appears to differ by race (significant SES × SAMPLE_RACE interaction, LR=9.57, df=2, p=0.008; per-1-SD-SES odds ratios: Black 2.07, Hispanic 1.65 vs White 1.18). However this apparent moderation is an artifact of racial differences in academic ability and class rank. After adjusting for ABILITY: COMPOSITE OF ASVAB SCORE, PERCENTILE IN CLASS, SAMPLE_SEX and FAMILY SIZE OF SAMPLE, the interaction is no longer significant (LR=1.75, df=2, p=0.42) and the per-race SES effects converge (per +1 SD SES: White OR 1.19 [0.99–1.43], Black OR 1.56 [1.08–2.26], Hispanic OR 1.20 [0.77–1.89]); no pairwise slope difference is significant. Firth penalized logistic regression (robust to the rare 2.69% outcome) reproduces these estimates almost exactly, and a probit link gives the same non-significant interaction (p=0.40). The Hispanic subgroup is too sparse (only 19 completions) for a stable SES estimate, so the robust core of the conclusion is the White-vs-Black contrast: both show a positive SES effect whose magnitudes are not significantly different.

Plain-language summary: SES predicts bachelor's-degree completion similarly across races; after accounting for ability and class rank, race itself does NOT meaningfully change the SES–degree relationship. The raw, unadjusted impression that the SES effect is "stronger for Black and Hispanic respondents" is explained by those groups' lower average academic ability and class rank, not by a genuine race-by-SES interaction.

payload.workflow: Loaded data/nls_ses_processed.csv (dropped the row-index column; 0 missing), converted BA DEGREE COMPLETED to 0/1, z-scored SES and the continuous covariates, created Black/Hispanic dummies (White reference) and a Male dummy. (1) Primary model: logistic regression BA ~ SES_z*(Black+Hispanic) + ABILITY_z + PERCENTILE_z + Male + FAMSIZ_z, with a joint df=2 likelihood-ratio test on the two SES x race interaction terms and per-race marginal SES effects (linear combinations of coefficients) reported as ORs with 95% CIs. (2) Sensitivity: minimal-adjustment model BA ~ SES_z*(Black+Hispanic) to separate the interaction from confounding. (3) Stratified per-race logistic models of SES_z -> BA (covariate-adjusted) plus pairwise slope-difference tests. (4) Robustness: probit-link re-fit of the full model and a Firth penalized logistic re-fit (numerical BFGS maximization of log-likelihood + 0.5*log|X'WX|, SEs from the inverse numerical Hessian) to guard against the rare-outcome/separation concern. Conclusion anchored on the White-vs-Black contrast given the sparse Hispanic cell (19 events).
